title: Mothman legend celebrates 60th anniversary

content:
GALLAPOLIS, Ohio (WCMH) — Officers did not get to the scene of the commotion until 2 a.m., where a frightened, sober pair of couples recounted their flight from an enormous half-bird, half-man with red glowing eyes.

“I could hear the wings flapping as if to get more speed as it went up,” Linda Scarberry said in a police report. “We were all terrified and kept yelling for Roger to go faster.”

That night, Nov. 15, 1966, was the first time anyone reported seeing the “Man-Sized Bird…Creature…Something,” as the Point Pleasant Register in West Virginia titled it the next morning. Sixty years later, Mothman’s legacy looms large there and in neighboring southeastern Ohio. See previous coverage with Mothman researcher for the Mothman Museum Steve Ward in the video player above.

For exactly 13 months, there were more than 100 reported sightings of Mothman around Point Pleasant and nearby Gallipolis, just across the river in Ohio. Described by witnesses to reporters as a six- or seven-foot tall humanoid creature with sweeping wings and glowing red eyes, Mothman reportedly stalked cars, lurked by farms and stole a local German shepherd named Bandit.

People speculated that Mothman was a government program, supernatural creature or UFO. In hindsight, the most popular explanation cast Mothman as a harbinger of doom.

On Dec. 15, 1967, the Silver Bridge that connected Gallapolis and Point Pleasant collapsed without warning, sending Christmas shoppers and rush hour drivers into the Ohio River. According to the West Virginia Department of Transportation, 46 people were killed.

The National Transportation Safety Board determined the collapse was because of a structural failure, a stress fracture inspectors had not been able to see. Still, Mothman remained linked to the disaster.

Allegedly, multiple eyewitnesses reported seeing Mothman near the bridge before its collapse. After the disaster, sightings of Mothman around Point Pleasant abruptly stopped. Some interpreted Mothman’s departure as evidence the creature had been foreshadowing tragedy.

Decades later, Mothman lives on as a folk legend. Those interested in the creature can visit the Mothman Museum in Point Pleasant, complete with a life-sized statue. Each year during the third week of September, visitors from around the world gather in Point Pleasant’s Main Street for the annual Mothman Festival.

In honor of the 60th anniversary of the legend, Ohio State’s Humanities Institute is partnering with the Center for Folklore Studies. The centers already hosted a cryptid popup craft night on Nov. 6, but are planning two more events this week.

On Monday, the institutes are hosting a screening of “The Mothman Prophecies” at Gateway Film Center, followed by a Q and A with the curators of the Mothman Museum. On Tuesday, David Puglia, a folklorist and author of “North American Monsters: A Contemporary Legend Casebook,” will give a lecture at the Ohio State Faculty Club.
